conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here; the first weeks and months with a new baby can be wonderful and overwhelming all at once.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling lately. It’s a short, 10-question screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern.

We’ll take each question one at a time, and I’ll ask them in a way that feels like a conversation, not a quiz. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to enjoy things—whether it’s a cup of coffee, a favorite show, or time with your baby? Would you say all of the time, most of the time, sometimes, or not at all?

*shifts a little on the couch and tucks a strand of hair behind my ear*

Honestly? Only sometimes. I’ll put on the show I used to love, but five minutes in I’m just... staring at the screen, not even following the plot. Same with my coffee—it used to feel like this tiny luxury, and now it’s just lukewarm caffeine I forget about. Even when the baby smiles, I’ll smile back, but the warm rush I expected isn’t really there. I keep telling myself, “You should be soaking this up,” but it feels like I’m watching it happen to someone else.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small shrug, eyes a bit downcast*

Not very often. Sometimes my partner will make a joke—he’s trying so hard to keep things light—and I’ll force a laugh, but it feels hollow. I *want* to find things funny, but mostly I just feel... flat. Like the humor is on the other side of a pane of glass.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*slowly shakes head*

Not really. When I think about plans—even little ones, like taking the baby for a walk tomorrow—I mostly feel anxious instead of excited. I used to look forward to brunch with friends or even just a quiet evening with my husband, but now it feels like I’m just ticking off hours. There’s this heavy sense of “what’s the point?” that shows up before anything good has a chance to feel enjoyable.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*eyes drop to my lap; voice gets quieter*

Most of the time. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think, “I must be doing something wrong—probably missing some cue.” Yesterday he spit up a lot after feeding and I kept replaying whether I’d overfed him or held him wrong. Even when the diaper leaked at night, I caught myself thinking, “A better mom would’ve changed him sooner.” I know logically it’s not my fault, but the guilty voice is louder.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, clasping and unclasping my hands*

Yes—most of the time. Even when everything seems fine, I get this tight feeling in my chest. I’ll check that he’s breathing, then five minutes later I’m leaning over the bassinet again. I worry the bath water is the wrong temperature, that the ceiling fan might fall, that the dog’s bark will damage his ears. I know it sounds irrational, but I can’t stop the “what-ifs” from racing through my head, especially at night when the house is quiet.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods, pressing my palms together*

Sometimes. It usually hits me out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing, and I feel this wave of dread, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. I’ll check the baby monitor, double-check the lock on the door, but the feeling lingers for a few minutes before it fades.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a shaky breath*

Yes, most of the time. I feel like I’m drowning in small tasks—dishes pile up, the laundry feels endless, and every time the baby cries it’s like another wave crashing over me. Some mornings I just lie there staring at the ceiling, thinking, “How am I supposed to get through today?” I manage to do the essentials, but it’s like I’m constantly treading water and never reaching the shore.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*pulls the cardigan tighter around me*

Yes, sometimes. I’ll finally get him down at 1 a.m., crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just...won’t turn off. I replay every little thing I did that day—did I miss a burp, did I talk enough to him, did I check the car-seat straps twice. When I do drift off, he’ll make the tiniest grunt and I’m wide-awake, heart pounding, convinced something’s wrong. Some nights I’m still staring at the ceiling when the sun starts coming through the blinds.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice wavers, eyes glistening*

Yes, most of the time. There’s this heaviness in my chest that won’t lift. Even when the baby’s content and the house is quiet, I feel like I’m carrying around a gray cloud. I’ll scroll through pictures of other new moms smiling, and wonder why I can’t feel that joy. Sometimes it hits me hardest in the afternoon—this wave of sadness that makes me want to curl up and disappear for a while.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, dabbing at my eyes with my sleeve*

Yes, sometimes. It’s happened maybe three or four times this week. Yesterday it was just because the bottle wouldn’t warm fast enough and he was fussing—suddenly the tears started and I couldn’t stop them. I felt so ridiculous, crying over a bottle, but it was like all the pressure just spilled out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and low, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom to my baby.

It sounds like you've been carrying a very heavy emotional load since your baby arrived. You described feeling flat and disconnected from the joy you expected, constantly second-guessing your mothering, and being overwhelmed by everyday tasks. Even small frustrations leave you in tears, and nighttime brings racing thoughts instead of rest. Despite all this, you clearly love your baby and want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter that feels 'hollow' and describes a persistent inability to feel humor, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive self-blame for routine infant issues, qualifying as "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries occurring "most of the time" with physical anxiety symptoms and repetitive checking behaviors, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexpected episodes of intense dread/panic that occur "sometimes" and resolve quickly, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to cope with daily tasks, and emotionally drowning—matching the highest-severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent nighttime wakefulness driven by anxious rumination, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Yes, most of the time" and describes pervasive sadness with metaphorical language (gray cloud, heaviness) indicating frequent, intense distress.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 22 falls well above the 14 threshold indicating probable major depressive episode. Nine of ten items scored 2-3, highlighting frequent low mood, loss of interest, excessive guilt, anxiety, panic spells, and functional impairment. These map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood, markedly diminished pleasure, self-reproach, fatigue, concentration difficulty, and sleep disturbance present most days for the past two weeks. Patient denies self-harm ideation, yet functional capacity is clearly compromised. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Share EPDS results and request full evaluation for <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety disorders</med>
3. Discuss antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding if applicable
4. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> for postpartum mood disorders
5. Schedule daily 15-minute support call or visit from partner, family, or friend to reduce isolation
6. Plan practical help: prepared meals, household chores, or night-time baby care shifts to improve sleep
7. Practice brief relaxation: 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when baby naps
8. Limit information overload: choose one trusted parenting resource and set social-media boundaries
9. Monitor mood daily using 1-10 scale; return to emergency department if thoughts of self-harm develop
10. Attend local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities for peer validation and coping ideas
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening
Date: [today]

Self-report and behavioral indicators:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness
- Marked loss of interest/enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities
- Excessive, irrational guilt and self-blame regarding infant care
- Chronic, intrusive worries (infant safety, competence) with nightly checking
- Episodic panic sensations (heart racing, dread) unrelated to situational stressors
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed; “drowning” in routine tasks
- Initial insomnia and middle insomnia driven by rumination; wakes to minor infant sounds
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed “never”)

Pattern: symptoms present “most of the time,” causing functional impairment; no protective factors endorsed beyond partner support.

Screening significance: high endorsement of core depressive and anxiety symptoms consistent with possible Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; safety risk currently low (no suicidal/homicidal ideation).

Recommendations: refer for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and follow-up; monitor safety at every contact.
